title: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions

subtopics.heading: Windows 10 editions
subtopics.notes:
Four editions:

- Home: consumer build. Integrates with Microsoft account + OneDrive backup. Includes Windows Defender antivirus and Cortana voice assistant. No domain join, no BitLocker, no RDP server, no gpedit, RDP client only
- Pro: enterprise build. Adds RDP server, BitLocker full disk encryption, domain join, gpedit
- Pro for Workstations: high-end. Up to four physical CPUs, 6 TB RAM, ReFS support
- Enterprise: volume-licensed at scale. Adds AppLocker (application allow/block), BranchCache (remote-site caching), and granular UX control

Microsoft has announced Windows 10 Home and Pro reach end of support on October 14, 2025.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Know which edition supports which feature - especially RDP server, BitLocker, and domain join. These are the differentiators most likely to appear.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming Home supports BitLocker. It does not. Windows 11 Home gets 'Device Encryption' (similar but consumer-grade); Windows 10 Home has neither.

subtopics.heading: Windows 11 editions
subtopics.notes:
Three editions: Home, Pro, Enterprise.

Windows 11 changes vs Windows 10:
- No 32-bit support at all (CPU must be 64-bit)
- New UI (start menu centered, new taskbar, snap layouts)
- Microsoft Teams integration
- Windows Copilot (AI assistant) built in
- Improved touch / tablet support

Per edition:
- Home: consumer build. Microsoft account or local account. Device Encryption (consumer BitLocker, recovery key stored in Microsoft account, not Active Directory)
- Pro: domain join, BitLocker, Hyper-V virtualization, RDP server
- Enterprise: MDM (Mobile Device Management), MAM (Mobile Application Management), ReFS support (same FS used in Windows Server)
subtopics.whyOnExam: Windows 11 Home has Device Encryption, NOT BitLocker. Pro is where BitLocker proper appears. ReFS is Enterprise-only on the desktop side.
subtopics.commonTrap: Mixing up Device Encryption and BitLocker. Both encrypt the disk, but only BitLocker (Pro+) integrates with Active Directory and is the 'business answer'.

subtopics.heading: N versions
subtopics.notes:
Windows N editions ship in Europe to comply with regulatory rulings. The 'N' means NO bundled media player or other multimedia utilities.

Media features can be added afterward via the Media Feature Pack:
Settings > Apps > Optional Features > Add an Optional Feature > Media Feature Pack
subtopics.whyOnExam: Just know what the 'N' means and that the Media Feature Pack restores playback. Low-yield trivia.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming N editions are crippled or different. They are functionally identical except for the bundled media components.

subtopics.heading: Feature differences across editions
subtopics.notes:
Cross-edition matrix (memorize the gates):

| Feature | Home | Pro | Pro Workstations | Enterprise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Domain join | NO | YES | YES | YES |
| BitLocker (full BL) | NO | YES | YES | YES |
| RDP as server (host) | NO | YES | YES | YES |
| RDP as client | YES | YES | YES | YES |
| gpedit.msc (group policy) | NO | YES | YES | YES |
| Max RAM (64-bit) | 128 GB | 2 TB | 6 TB | 6 TB |

Windows 10 Home (32-bit) tops out at 4 GB RAM. Windows 11 has no 32-bit version at all.

Domain vs workgroup:
- Domain: central management via Active Directory, used at work
- Workgroup: each device managed independently, used at home
subtopics.whyOnExam: This matrix shows up directly in exam questions. The 'four big gates' between Home and Pro are domain join, BitLocker, RDP server, and gpedit.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking Pro when the scenario clearly needs 6 TB of RAM (which only Pro Workstations / Enterprise supports). Pro caps at 2 TB.

subtopics.heading: Upgrade paths and hardware requirements
subtopics.notes:
Upgrade paths:
- In-place upgrade: keep apps, data, settings. Run from inside the existing OS
- Clean install: wipe and install fresh. Boot from media

Windows 11 hardware requirements:
- TPM 2.0
- UEFI BIOS
- Secure Boot enabled
- 64-bit CPU only (no 32-bit support)

Use PC Health Check to confirm compatibility before attempting the upgrade.
subtopics.whyOnExam: TPM 2.0 + UEFI + Secure Boot is the Windows 11 trifecta. Memorize all three.
subtopics.commonTrap: Believing a CPU upgrade alone makes a system Windows 11-eligible. The motherboard must also provide TPM 2.0 and UEFI/Secure Boot.
